In recent days, a series of technical outages have grounded planes, closed bank accounts, shut us out of our email and generally created a sense that the world is either falling apart or being hacked, or maybe both.
The New York Times reporters Karoun Demirjian, Dustin Volz and Zolan Kanno-Youngs explain what’s really going on and whether we can expect it to continue.
Guest:
Karoun Demirjian, a breaking news reporter for the The New York Times.Dustin Volz, a cybersecurity and intelligence reporter for The New York Times.Zolan Kanno-Youngs, a White House correspondent for The New York Times.Background reading: 
Widespread technology outages put a focus on President Trump’s national security cuts.A ground stop for flights came as Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy pushed to rapidly upgrade aviation systems.Photo: Alex Kent/The New York Times

Anthropic is a barometer of the economy at a volatile time. Its initial public offering will have widespread implications. 
As Anthropic prepares for what is expected to be a huge initial public offering this week, the company has been wooing investors with a simple message: Bet on us. But Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation from Nvidia last week raised questions about the stability of the entire artificial intelligence industry.
Erin Griffith, a tech reporter for The New York Times, explains why Anthropic’s I.P.O. is a litmus test for the future of A.I.
Guest: Erin Griffith, a technology reporter for The New York Times.
Background reading: 
Anthropic is targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for its blockbuster I.P.O., a pricing that would make it one of the biggest public listings.What’s riding on Anthropic’s market debut? Nearly everything.Photo: Andres Kudacki for The New York Times

results.description:
Thursday, Nov. 19 will see the release of one of the biggest, most anticipated entertainment properties of the year: The video game Grand Theft Auto VI.
The first Grand Theft Auto game was released in 1997, and immediately stoked controversy with its aggressively satirical portrait of amoral, criminal American culture. Over the past 30 years, the franchise has continued to keep a sharp satirical eye on American society, and its often unpleasant excesses. The sixth installment promises to touch on hot-button issues like the war on drugs, police violence, conspiracy theories and influencer culture. And yet, even though the game has already made one billion dollars in pre-order sales, it might be the last time we ever see one of this scale.
In this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” Michael Barbaro talks with reporter Zachary Small, who covers video games for The Times, about Grand Theft Auto and how it became one of the biggest video game franchises of all time.
 
On Today’s Episode
Zachary Small is a New York Times reporter writing about the art world’s relationship to money, politics and technology.
